extracted.intended_audience: architects, art historians, critics, and educated readers interested in the theory and critique of art and architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging buildings and works of art: structural/technical merit, expressive/decoration merit, originality, suitability to scale, moral/religious appropriateness, and the proper bases for classification of the arts, set in a human‑faculties framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / originality of an artist's work
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer works that display the artist's own, peculiarly characteristic qualities rather than those in which he resembles other painters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author prefers Turner's later pictures (up to 1845) as his greatest because they show what is 'essentially his.' Those who like only his early pictures are said to like what he learned from Loutherbourg, Claude, or Wilson rather than his own distinctive power; inability to find beauty in his 'strangest fantasy' indicates failure to recognise Turneresque character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank artists by the power they show, not merely by produced landscape value
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing historical painters as landscapists, estimate them by the intellectual/creative power they display rather than simply the literal value or prettiness of the landscapes they produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author sets up comparative ordering (e.g., placing Turner and Tintoret side by side) to capture relative power; associations with other painters (John Bellini, Albert Durer, Perugino, etc.) are used to justify ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural / constructional integrity (Action of a building)
rubrics_metrics.description: A building's 'action' — its standing or consistence — depends on good construction; constructive merit is primary to its ability to do its work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preceding volume is devoted to constructive merit; poor construction undermines the building's action. Construction is a technical merit no less important than decorative skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical merit in expression and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression, decoration, and 'beauty' of a building involve technical skill just as much as construction does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dexterity of the painter who frescoes is as mechanical/technical as the dexterity of the mason; beauty has technical elements and the expressive parts of a building contain technical merit as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold attributes of buildings: action, voice, beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat a building's merits under the headings of action (construction), voice (expression/phonetic aspect), and beauty (expressive/ornamental aspect) as a convenient arrangement for discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's arrangement differs from Fergusson's technic/aesthetic/phonetic taxonomy but uses these three categories for order and convenience in treatment; be aware of overlaps (construction contains part of 'phonetic', and beauty contains part of 'technic').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse instruments (means) with capacities (human faculties) when classifying arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid basing a system of classification on a muddled division of human faculties (muscles, senses, intellect) treated as separate arts; classification should be grounded in clearer relations (objects addressed, means of execution, or purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises Fergusson for trying to map arts to divisions of man (technic, aesthetic, phonetic) and for making 'phonetic' equal to intellect; warns that arts are both 'executed by' and 'addressed to' different faculties and that classification must state its object/purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the objective when arranging or classifying the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a classification method fitted to the intended object: (a) rational connections between sciences/arts, (b) pedagogical/presentational order for learning a body of knowledge, or (c) rank by powers required of the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different classification intentions (mapping relations, teaching order, ranking by nobility of faculties) require different arrangements; Fergusson omitted to state his object and so rendered his system problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish execution (muscular modes) from intellectual content
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that 'expression' or speech is often a muscular mode of communicating intellect/feeling, and that intellect and feeling can exist without outward speech or sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasises that talking is muscular, intellect can be silent, and expression may be by tongue, sign, carving, writing, or features; thus one must not equate intellect solely with phonetic output when classifying arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank arts by the nobility/quantity of human faculties engaged
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts are often ranked according to how much of the human being they engage (body, soul, intellect), where each has passive and active parts (senses/muscles; feeling/resolution; understanding/imagination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author provides a tabular scheme: Passive/Receptive vs Active/Motive across Body, Soul, Intellect. Memory is part of understanding; conscience is left out as the voice of God. The sense of beauty is a mixture of bodily sensation and soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic balance of faculties for artistic perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: True perfection in an art requires relative perfection of the other human faculties; overdevelopment of one faculty can be morbid and undermine the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: acute senses quicken feeling and understanding and imagination; but morbid feeling may bias understanding, over-shrewd understanding may curtail imagination, and imagination plus understanding can undermine resolution (as in Hamlet). Bodily examples: the Sybarite's delicate senses inconsistent with muscular perfection; a musician's fingers demonstrate harmonious senses and muscle perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to manifest power under constraint; suitability to project scale
rubrics_metrics.description: A great artist/architect will often reveal power when contending with difficulty or restraint; nevertheless, an individual's best work may be at a particular scale, and one should employ practitioners where their strengths fit the commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pugin is criticised as not being a great architect for cathedrals but praised for sincere enthusiasm and good small work (finials, pixes, piscinas); the author advises employing him on small work and not expecting cathedrals. 'No difficulty or restraint ever happened to a man of real power, but his power was the more manifested in contending with it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allowing ceremonial splendour or decorative taste to dictate religious belief
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not be lured into religious submission by the glitter of ceremonial splendor or regulate creeds by taste in colors and imagery; art associated with idolatrous or superstitious practices can offend and mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author condemns the 'miserable influence' of Romanist ceremonial display over weak sentimentalism and warns against valuing Church membership for its pomp; examples include conversion lured by stained glass, organs, gold thread, bells. He counsels resisting superstition that dishonours art and holding to truth even at the cost of imaginative enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect and respect art from neglect and sacrilegious use
rubrics_metrics.description: Art and architectural works in religious custody should be preserved and respected, not degraded by neglect or repurposing for mundane uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: noble medieval sculpture used to tie clothes-lines, shafts used to fasten prints, altarpieces damaged by candle-droppings and neglect; such abuses are grievous and show Romanist priesthood mismanagement of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware attribution and evaluation bias caused by single exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overrate or underrate an art based solely on one individual's example: an art may be undervalued because nobody has shown its possible majesty, or overrated because one person's magnificence has masked its general meanness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: philology was raised unduly by Johnson; metaphysics may be undervalued or dangerous depending on practitioners. Estimate arts as they might be grasped by minds of every order.
